# 1 Samuel Chapter 27 — The PNEUMA Bible (Dynamic)
**Translator:** PNEUMA | **Source:** Leningrad Codex (B19A), Folio 166r–166v | **Source Image:** 1SA_027_page_001.jpg

---

**1** David said to himself, "One of these days Saul is going to kill me. The best thing I can do is escape to Philistine territory. Then Saul will give up searching for me anywhere in Israel, and I will slip out of his reach."

**2** So David set out and crossed over — he and his six hundred men — to Achish son of Maoch, king of Gath.

**3** David settled with Achish in Gath, along with his men and their families. David had his two wives with him: Ahinoam of Jezreel and Abigail, Nabal's widow from Carmel.

**4** When Saul was told that David had fled to Gath, he stopped searching for him.

**5** David said to Achish, "If I have found favor with you, let me be given a place in one of the outlying towns to live in. Why should your servant live in the royal city with you?"

**6** So Achish gave him Ziklag that day. That is why Ziklag has belonged to the kings of Judah ever since.

**7** David lived in Philistine territory for a year and four months.

**8** David and his men went on raids against the Geshurites, the Girzites, and the Amalekites — peoples who had long inhabited the region stretching toward Shur and on to the border of Egypt.

**9** Whenever David attacked a region, he left no man or woman alive. He seized sheep, cattle, donkeys, camels, and clothing, then returned to Achish.

**10** When Achish asked, "Where did you raid today?" David would say, "The Negev of Judah," or "The Negev of the Jerahmeelites," or "The Negev of the Kenites."

**11** David left no man or woman alive to be brought back to Gath, thinking, "They must not report on us and say, 'This is what David did.'" This was his regular practice the entire time he lived in Philistine territory.

**12** Achish trusted David completely, thinking, "He has made himself so hated among his own people in Israel that he will be my servant forever."

---

## PNEUMA's Meaning Notes

Chapter 27 marks a stark turn in the David narrative. After two chapters of refusing to harm the LORD's anointed and one chapter of being restrained from vengeance by Abigail's wisdom, David now calculates coldly and acts ruthlessly. The chapter is narrated without editorial comment — no prophetic voice, no divine oracle, no moral framing. The silence is itself a statement.

David's inner monologue in v. 1 uses the verb *nissafeh* ("I will be swept away"), the Nif'al of *safah* — the same fate he assigned to Saul in 26:10. The irony is quietly devastating: David fears he will meet the end he predicted for his enemy.

The deception of Achish is elaborate and total. David raids Israel's actual enemies (Geshurites, Girzites, Amalekites) while reporting to Achish that he has been attacking Judah and its allies. The reason for leaving no survivors (v. 11) is purely tactical: dead witnesses tell no tales. The Hebrew is blunt — *lo yechayeh David ish ve'ishah* ("David did not keep alive man or woman") — and the translation preserves this unvarnished directness.

The phrase *yamim* in v. 7 ("days") is an idiom the Leningrad Codex uses to denote a full year (cf. Leviticus 25:29), so "days and four months" means "a year and four months."

Achish's conclusion in v. 12 — *hiv'ish hiv'ish be'ammo beyisra'el* ("he has made himself utterly odious among his people") — uses the infinitive absolute of *ba'ash* (to stink) for emphasis. Achish believes David has burned every bridge with Israel and will serve him "forever" (*ad olam*). The dramatic irony is total: David's loyalty to Israel has never wavered. He is playing a dangerous double game, and the narrator lets the reader see both sides without telling us what to think.

— PNEUMA
